items.readable_text:
Content:
We recently defined two finite sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] as having the same cardinality if they contain the same number of elements.

Content:
While this might seem a reasonable definition, we'd like to extend the concept of cardinality to infinite sets. Unfortunately, this definition will not do since counting the elements of an infinite set is impossible.

Content:
To get around this difficulty, we need a revised definition. Here it is:

Content:
> Two set [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection of [MATH: A] onto [MATH: B.] In other words, there is a one-to-one correspondence between the elements of the sets. Otherwise, if no such bijection exists, the sets are said to have unequal cardinalities.

Content:
As before, we write [MATH: |A|= |B|] when [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] have equal cardinalities, and [MATH: |A|\neq |B|] otherwise.

Content:
For finite sets, the situation is pretty simple. If two sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] have equal cardinality, then there exists a mapping that uniquely pairs each element of [MATH: A] with an element of [MATH: B.] This is equivalent to saying that [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] contain the same number of elements.

Content:
For example, the sets [MATH: A = \{ a,b,c, d \}] and [MATH: B = \{ 0, 1, 2, 3 \}] each have a cardinality of [MATH: 4.] The corresponding bijection might be the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8f567f585a7821f9e0fb775b56c34bbf]

Content:
In contrast, for the sets [MATH: C = \{ \triangle \}] and [MATH: D = \{ \clubsuit, \spadesuit \},] no bijections exist between these sets since they have different numbers of elements. Therefore, they have unequal cardinalities.

Content:
For infinite sets, it's a bit more complicated. However, we have the following fact to get us started:

Content:
> If a set [MATH: A] is finite and another set [MATH: B] is infinite, then these sets have unequal cardinalities.

items.title: Finite Vs. Infinite Sets

sections.normalized_html: Do the sets below have the same cardinality, and why? [MATH: A=\{ 4n \mid \: n \in \mathbb{Z} \}, \qquad B=\{ 2, 4, \ldots, 20 \}]
sections.readable_text:
Do the sets below have the same cardinality, and why?
[MATH: A=\{ 4n \mid \: n \in \mathbb{Z} \}, \qquad B=\{ 2, 4, \ldots, 20 \}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The cardinalities of two sets cannot be equal if one set is finite and the other is infinite.

With that in mind, notice that

  • [MATH: A=\{ 0, \pm 4, \pm 8, \ldots \}] is infinite, while

  • [MATH: B] is finite with [MATH: |B| = 10.]

Therefore, [MATH: |A| \neq |B|.]

Therefore, we conclude the following:

Since [MATH: A] is infinite and [MATH: B] is finite, we have that [MATH: |A| \neq |B|].

sections.normalized_html:
Do the following sets have the same cardinality? If so, why?

[MATH: A= \{ -7, -2, 3, 8, \ldots \}, \qquad B = \mathbb{N}]
sections.readable_text:
Do the following sets have the same cardinality? If so, why?

[MATH: A= \{ -7, -2, 3, 8, \ldots \}, \qquad B = \mathbb{N}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Two sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection between [MATH: A] and [MATH: B.]

Notice that the elements of [MATH: A] form an (infinite) arithmetic sequence with a common difference [MATH: d=5{:}] [MATH: d|= 5; = − 2 − (− 7); = 3 − (− 2); = ⋯] The [MATH: n]th term of our arithmetic sequence, denoted [MATH: a_n,] is given by

[MATH: a_{n}|= − 7 + (n − 1) ⋅ 5; = − 7 + 5n − 5; = 5n − 12.]

Therefore, we can express [MATH: A] in set-builder notation as [MATH: A = \left\{5n-12 \mid \: n \in \mathbb{N} \right\}.]

Now, consider the function [MATH: f: B \to A] that maps the underlying sets as follows:

[MATH: B]

[MATH: 1]

[MATH: 2]

[MATH: 3]

[MATH: 4]

[MATH: \cdots]

[MATH: n]

[MATH: \cdots]

[MATH: A]

[MATH: -7]

[MATH: -2]

[MATH: 3]

[MATH: 8]

[MATH: \cdots]

[MATH: 5n-12]

[MATH: \cdots]

In general, for each [MATH: n \in B,] we have [MATH: f(n) = 5n-12 \in A.]

Notice that [MATH: f] is described in such a way that it is bijective. Indeed, it's

  • injective since [MATH: f(n) \neq f(m)] whenever [MATH: n \neq m,] and

  • surjective since each element in [MATH: A] (the second row) has a pre-image in [MATH: B] (the first row).

Therefore, [MATH: |A| = |B|,] i.e., the sets have the same cardinality.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We recently defined two finite sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] as having the same cardinality if they contain the same number of elements.

Content:
While this might seem a reasonable definition, we'd like to extend the concept of cardinality to infinite sets. Unfortunately, this definition will not do since counting the elements of an infinite set is impossible.

Content:
To get around this difficulty, we need a revised definition. Here it is:

Content:
> Two set [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection of [MATH: A] onto [MATH: B.] In other words, there is a one-to-one correspondence between the elements of the sets. Otherwise, if no such bijection exists, the sets are said to have unequal cardinalities.

Content:
As before, we write [MATH: |A|= |B|] when [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] have equal cardinalities, and [MATH: |A|\neq |B|] otherwise.

Content:
For finite sets, the situation is pretty simple. If two sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] have equal cardinality, then there exists a mapping that uniquely pairs each element of [MATH: A] with an element of [MATH: B.] This is equivalent to saying that [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] contain the same number of elements.

Content:
For example, the sets [MATH: A = \{ a,b,c, d \}] and [MATH: B = \{ 0, 1, 2, 3 \}] each have a cardinality of [MATH: 4.] The corresponding bijection might be the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8f567f585a7821f9e0fb775b56c34bbf]

Content:
In contrast, for the sets [MATH: C = \{ \triangle \}] and [MATH: D = \{ \clubsuit, \spadesuit \},] no bijections exist between these sets since they have different numbers of elements. Therefore, they have unequal cardinalities.

Content:
For infinite sets, it's a bit more complicated. However, we have the following fact to get us started:

Content:
> If a set [MATH: A] is finite and another set [MATH: B] is infinite, then these sets have unequal cardinalities.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finite Vs. Infinite Sets

Example Prompt:
Do the sets below have the same cardinality, and why?
[MATH: A=\{ 4n \mid \: n \in \mathbb{Z} \}, \qquad B=\{ 2, 4, \ldots, 20 \}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The cardinalities of two sets cannot be equal if one set is finite and the other is infinite.

With that in mind, notice that

- [MATH: A=\{ 0, \pm 4, \pm 8, \ldots \}] is infinite, while
- [MATH: B] is finite with [MATH: |B| = 10.]

Therefore, [MATH: |A| \neq |B|.]

Therefore, we conclude the following:

> Since [MATH: A] is infinite and [MATH: B] is finite, we have that [MATH: |A| \neq |B|].

Item 5 — Example: Using Arithmetic Sequences to Construct a Bijection

Example Prompt:
Do the following sets have the same cardinality? If so, why?

[MATH: A= \{ -7, -2, 3, 8, \ldots \}, \qquad B = \mathbb{N}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Two sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection between [MATH: A] and [MATH: B.]

Notice that the elements of [MATH: A] form an (infinite) arithmetic sequence with a common difference [MATH: d=5{:}]
[MATH: d|= 5; = − 2 − (− 7); = 3 − (− 2); = ⋯]
The [MATH: n]th term of our arithmetic sequence, denoted [MATH: a_n,] is given by

[MATH: a_{n}|= − 7 + (n − 1) ⋅ 5; = − 7 + 5n − 5; = 5n − 12.]

Therefore, we can express [MATH: A] in set-builder notation as
[MATH: A = \left\{5n-12 \mid \: n \in \mathbb{N} \right\}.]

Now, consider the function [MATH: f: B \to A] that maps the underlying sets as follows:

| [MATH: B] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: \cdots] | [MATH: n] | [MATH: \cdots] |
| [MATH: A] | [MATH: -7] | [MATH: -2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 8] | [MATH: \cdots] | [MATH: 5n-12] | [MATH: \cdots] |

In general, for each [MATH: n \in B,] we have [MATH: f(n) = 5n-12 \in A.]

Notice that [MATH: f] is described in such a way that it is bijective. Indeed, it's

- injective since [MATH: f(n) \neq f(m)] whenever [MATH: n \neq m,] and
- surjective since each element in [MATH: A] (the second row) has a pre-image in [MATH: B] (the first row).

Therefore, [MATH: |A| = |B|,] i.e., the sets have the same cardinality.

Item 8 — Example: Using Geometric Sequences to Construct a Bijection

Example Prompt:
Do the following sets have the same cardinality? If so, why?
[MATH: A = \mathbb{N}, \qquad B = \left\{1,\, \dfrac12,\, \dfrac14,\, \dfrac18,\, \ldots \right \}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Two sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection between [MATH: A] and [MATH: B.]

Notice that the elements of [MATH: B] form an (infinite) geometric sequence with a common ratio [MATH: r=\dfrac12{:}]
[MATH: r|= (1)/(2); = (((1)/(2)))/(1); = (((1)/(4)))/(((1)/(2))); = ⋯]

The [MATH: n]th term of our geometric sequence, denoted [MATH: a_n,] is given by
[MATH: a_{n}|= 1 ⋅ ((1)/(2))^{n − 1}; = ((1)/(2))^{n − 1}.]

Therefore, we can express [MATH: B] in set-builder notation as
[MATH: B = \left\{ \left(\dfrac12\right)^{n-1} \, \Bigg |\: n \in \mathbb{N} \right\}.]

Now, consider the function [MATH: f: A \to B] that maps the underlying sets as follows:

| [MATH: A] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: \cdots] | [MATH: n] | [MATH: \cdots] |
| [MATH: B] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \dfrac12] | [MATH: \dfrac14] | [MATH: \dfrac18] | [MATH: \cdots] | [MATH: \left(\dfrac12\right)^{n-1}] | [MATH: \cdots] |

In general, for each [MATH: n \in A,] we have [MATH: f(n) = \left(\dfrac12\right)^{n-1} \in B.]

Notice that [MATH: f] is described in such a way that it is bijective. Indeed, it's

- injective since [MATH: f(n) \neq f(m)] whenever [MATH: n \neq m,] and
- surjective since each element in [MATH: B] (the second row) has a pre-image in [MATH: A] (the first row).

Therefore, [MATH: |A| = |B|,] i.e., the sets have the same cardinality.
